entries.label: Uses interval notation for a set that is not every real number in a stretch
entries.description: The student treats interval notation as a shorthand for any set that has a start and an end, so writes a set made of only some numbers in the stretch (such as only the whole numbers) as an interval like $[-13, 4)$.

refutation.text_md: You have spotted that interval notation, like $[-13, 4)$, is a quick way to write a stretch of numbers from one end to the other, and you want to use it for any set that starts and stops somewhere. That is a sensible idea, and it is right for one kind of set. The catch is which numbers the interval contains.

Interval notation can only be used to represent an interval of real numbers. So $[-13, 4)$ means every real number from $-13$ up to, but not including, $4$. That is not just the whole numbers: it also contains $-12.5$, $\frac{1}{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $3.999$ and every other real number in that stretch.

That is exactly what the $x\in\mathbb{R}$ says in set notation. $\{x:x\in\mathbb{R},-13\le x<4\}$ and $[-13, 4)$ name the same set. A set that keeps only some of the numbers in that stretch, such as only the whole numbers, leaves out $-12.5$ and all the others, so it is a different set and the interval $[-13, 4)$ cannot stand for it.

Before you write an interval, check that the set is every real number between the two ends, which in set notation shows up as $x\in\mathbb{R}$. If it is, convert it as in the examples, for instance $\{k:k\in\mathbb{R},-5<k<5\}$ becomes $(-5, 5)$. If the set is not a stretch of real numbers, interval notation is not the notation to use for it.

entries.label: Expects the output of k(x) = 3 to depend on the input
entries.description: Given a function whose rule is only a number, such as $k(x)=3$, the student hunts for an $x$ to use and builds an answer from the input (for example $3\times100=300$ for $k(100)$) instead of giving the number itself.
entries.signal: A value built from the input instead of 3: for $k(x)=3$, an answer to $k(100)$ such as 300, 103 or 100; for $k(f(6))$, an answer built from 37 such as 111 or 37.

refutation.text_md: Looking for where the input goes is the right habit: in $f(x)=x^2+1$ the input replaces $x$. Here the rule is $k(x)=3$, and there is no $x$ on the right-hand side for the input to replace.

So the input has nothing to change. Whatever number goes in, the rule only ever says "3", which is why $k(100)=3$. An answer like 300 would need a rule such as $3x$, and that is not the function you were given.
The same thing happens when the input is itself an answer from another function: once $f(6)=37$ is found, $k(f(6))=k(37)=3$. The 37 goes in and still does not appear in the output.
The move: replace $x$ only where $x$ actually appears in the rule. If the rule has no $x$, the output is that number whatever the input, so write it down: the output is always 3.

entries.label: Applies the two functions in the wrong order
entries.description: In something like $f(g(1))$ the student feeds the input into the function written first (outside) instead of evaluating the function inside the brackets first and passing its answer to the other function.
entries.signal: With $f(x)=x^2+1$ and $g(x)=x-4$, $f(g(1))$ answered as -2 (that is $g(f(1))$ instead of 10). With $k(x)=3$, $k(f(6))$ answered as 10 (that is $f(k(6))$ instead of 3).

refutation.text_md: You used both functions and you used every number, so the pieces are right. The slip is the order: in $f(g(1))$ the number $1$ is the input of $g$, not of $f$.
The book works from the inside out. With $f(x)=x^2+1$ and $g(x)=x-4$: first $g(1)=(1)-4=-3$. Only then does $-3$ become the input of $f$: $f(-3)=(-3)^2+1=10$.

Swapping the order is a different calculation. Putting $1$ into $f$ first gives $f(1)=2$, and then $g(2)=2-4=-2$. That is $g(f(1))$, and $-2$ does not match $f(g(1))=10$. The same happens with $k(f(6))$: $f(6)=37$ and $k(37)=3$, whereas doing $k$ first gives $k(6)=3$ and then $f(3)=10$.
The move: find the function inside the brackets first, write its answer down (here $g(1)=-3$), then rewrite the expression with that number as the input of the outer function ($f(-3)$) and evaluate.

entries.label: Splits the minus sign off a negative input
entries.description: When the input is negative, the student writes the minus sign outside the rule instead of substituting the whole input in brackets, for example $-1^2+1$ for $f(-1)$ when $f(x)=x^2+1$, so only the 1 is squared.
entries.signal: With $f(x)=x^2+1$, $f(-1)$ answered as 0 instead of 2: a squared negative input comes out negative.

refutation.text_md: You picked the right input, $-1$, and the rest of the rule is right. What went wrong is that the minus sign got separated from the $1$ before the squaring.
$x$ stands for the whole input, minus sign included. That is why the book puts the input in brackets as it substitutes: $f(-1)=(-1)^2+1$.

Now the bracket is worked out as one number: $(-1)^2=(-1)(-1)=1$, so $f(-1)=1+1=2$. Squaring only the $1$ and keeping the minus sign outside gives $-1+1=0$, which is not the same calculation and does not match $f(-1)=2$.
The move: write the input in brackets where $x$ was, work out the bracket as a whole, then finish the rest of the rule.

entries.label: Domain and range read from the wrong axes
entries.description: The student gives the lowest-to-highest $s$ values as the domain and the lowest-to-highest $t$ values as the range, so each is read off the wrong axis.
entries.signal: A domain written in distance values (for example $0 \le s \le 10$ for the ball, or $0 \le s \le 100$ for the car), or a range written in time values.

refutation.text_md: You have read a lowest and a highest value off the graph, which is the right kind of answer. Only the names are swapped: the values of one axis have been called the domain when they belong to the range, or the other way round.

Take a graph of a ball rolling down a $10$ m slope, with time $t$ in seconds along the bottom and distance $s(t)$ in metres up the side. The domain is the time values the graph covers: $0 \le t \le 20$, from $0$ s to $20$ s. The range is the distance values it covers: $0 \le s(t) \le 10$, from $0$ m to $10$ m.

If you wrote $0$ to $10$ as the domain, you described the distance, not the time. The meaning shows the slip too. That domain stands for the total time taken to reach the bottom of the slope, which is $20$ s, not $10$. In a graph of the distance travelled by a car, the range stands for the total distance travelled.

Before you write either one, look at which letter you are describing. The domain is the $t$ values the graph covers and the range is the $s$ values. Write each as a lowest-to-highest inequality with its units, then say what it represents.

entries.label: Takes the falling graph as the distance already rolled
entries.description: The student treats the height of the ball's line as the distance the ball has already rolled, so after reading the value at the given time they subtract it from the length of the slope instead of seeing it is already the distance still to roll.
entries.signal: An answer of $3$ m ($10 - 7$) to how much further the ball has to roll after $6$ s.

refutation.text_md: You read the graph at the right time, $t = 6$ s, and found that the line is at $7$. The slip is in what that $7$ measures: you took it as the distance the ball has already rolled, and so you worked out $10 - 7 = 3$ m.

Look at the two ends of the line. At $t = 0$, before the ball has moved, the line is at $10$ m. If $s(t)$ were the distance already rolled, it would be at $0$ there, because the ball has not rolled anywhere yet.

At $t = 20$ s, which is the total time the ball takes to reach the bottom of the slope, the line is at $0$ m. So $s(t)$ is the distance still left on the slope: it starts at $10$ m, with the whole slope ahead, and falls to $0$ m at the bottom.

That means the value you read, $7$ m at $6$ s, is already the answer to how much further the ball has to roll. No subtraction is needed. Before you subtract, check what the line's value means at the start and at the end of the graph, then answer from that reading: $7$ m.

entries.label: Takes 'an hour' as $t = 1$ when $t$ is in minutes
entries.description: The student reads the car's graph at $t = 1$ for 'an hour', forgetting that $t$ is measured in minutes, so one hour is $t = 60$.

refutation.text_md: Looking for 'an hour' on the graph is the right idea. The slip is that the axis labelled $t$ is not counted in hours. The question says $t$ is time in minutes, so $t = 1$ is one minute, not one hour.

Change the time into the graph's own unit first: one hour is $60$ minutes, so you need the point where $t = 60$. If you read the line at $t = 1$ instead, you get the distance after one minute, which on this graph is very close to $0$ km.
Find $60$ on the $t$ axis, go up to the line and read across to the $s(t)$ axis. The line is at $50$. Since $s(t)$ is in km, the car travelled $50$ km in an hour.
Whenever a question gives a time in different units from the axis, convert it to the axis's units before you read the graph. Then read the value and give it with the units of $s(t)$.

entries.label: Reads m and c before dividing by the number in front of y
entries.description: Takes the number in front of $x$ as the gradient, or the number on its own as the $y$-intercept, straight from an equation such as $2y=3x-6$ or $-y=x+2$, without first dividing both sides by whatever multiplies $y$.
entries.signal: A gradient that is just the number in front of $x$ (for example $3$ for $2y=3x-1$), an intercept that is just the number at the end (for example $6$ or $-6$ for $2y=3x-6$), or a gradient of $1$ for $-y=x+2$.

refutation.text_md: You read $m$ and $c$ straight off the equation as it is written. That is a sensible habit, because in $y=mx+c$ the gradient is the number in front of $x$ and the $y$-intercept is the number on its own. It only works once $y$ is completely alone on the left.
Take $2y=3x-6$. Reading straight off gives $3$ and $-6$, but the left side is $2y$, not $y$, so those numbers describe $2y$.
Divide both sides by $2$, so the number at the end is divided too: $y=\frac{3}{2}x-3$. Now $m=\frac{3}{2}$ and $c=-3$, and neither is the number you first saw.
A minus sign on $y$ works the same way. In $-y=x+2$, divide both sides by $-1$ and every sign flips: $y=-x-2$. The gradient is $-1$, not $1$.
So first get $y$ alone: divide both sides by whatever multiplies $y$, the number at the end included. Only then read $m$ from the number in front of $x$ and $c$ from the number on its own.

entries.label: Keeps a number's sign when it crosses the equals sign
entries.description: In an equation such as $y+5=x$, takes the $5$ sitting beside $y$ as the $y$-intercept, instead of moving it to the other side where it becomes $-5$.
entries.signal: A $y$-intercept with the opposite sign to the correct one, for example $5$ for $y+5=x$.

refutation.text_md: You saw the $5$ in $y+5=x$ and took it as the $y$-intercept. The $5$ is a real part of the equation, but it sits beside $y$ on the left, and $c$ can only be read once $y$ stands alone.
To get $y$ alone, take $5$ away from both sides: $y=x-5$. The $+5$ on the left became $-5$ on the right, so the $y$-intercept is $-5$.
A number changes sign when it crosses the equals sign. For example, $y+2x-3=1$ becomes $y=-2x+4$: the $+2x$ turns into $-2x$, and the $-3$ turns into $+3$, which is added to the $1$.
So before you read $c$, move everything except $y$ to the right, changing each sign as it crosses. The number left on its own is $c$.

entries.label: Swaps the jobs of m and c
entries.description: Calls the number on its own at the end of $y=mx+c$ the gradient (or the number beside $x$ the $y$-intercept), so $m$ and $c$ trade places.
entries.signal: A gradient equal to the number at the end of the equation, for example $-1$ for $y=\frac{1}{2}x-1$.

refutation.text_md: A common mix-up is to swap the two jobs: the number at the end gets called the gradient, and the number beside $x$ gets called the $y$-intercept. Both numbers are real and you have found them. They just do different jobs.
In $y=mx+c$, $m$ is multiplied by $x$, so it is the number in front of $x$. $c$ stands on its own with no $x$ next to it, and it is the $y$-intercept.
In $y=\frac{1}{2}x-1$, the number in front of $x$ is $\frac{1}{2}$, so $m=\frac{1}{2}$. The number on its own is $-1$, so $c=-1$. The gradient is $\frac{1}{2}$, not $-1$.
It works the same the other way round. In $y=x+4$ the $4$ stands on its own, so $c=4$, and the $y$-intercept is $4$.
To keep them apart, ask of each number: does it multiply $x$? Then it is $m$, the gradient. Does it stand on its own? Then it is $c$, the $y$-intercept.

entries.label: Thinks the straight-line form needs the letters m and c
entries.description: Says $y=ax+q$ is not a straight line because it is not written with the letters $m$ and $c$.
entries.signal: Says that $y=ax+q$ is not a straight line, or asks whether it is a different kind of equation from $y=mx+c$.

refutation.text_md: You may have felt that the straight-line form has to use the letters $m$ and $c$, so $y=ax+q$ looked like something else. It is fair to check, but the thing to check is the shape of the equation, not the letters.

Letters are only names for numbers. The pattern in $y=mx+c$ is: $y$ equals a number times $x$, plus or minus a number. $y=ax+q$ has the same pattern, with $a$ standing where $m$ stands and $q$ standing where $c$ stands.

Whatever numbers go in those two places, the graph is a straight line. $y=3x-1$, $y=-\frac{3}{4}x+3$ and $y=x-4$ all have this pattern, and all three graph as straight lines. Writing $a$ and $q$ in place of the numbers does not change the shape.
So when a statement uses other letters, check the pattern: a number times $x$, plus or minus a number. That is a straight line, so a function of the form $y=ax+q$ is one.

entries.label: Sets y = 0 to find the y-intercept
entries.description: The student reverses which letter to set to zero, using y = 0 for the y-intercept (and x = 0 for the x-intercept), so the two intercepts come out the wrong way round.
entries.signal: The value given as the y-intercept is really the x-intercept and the value given as the x-intercept is really the y-intercept (the two numbers swapped), or the statement 'let x = 0 to find the y-intercept' is marked false.

refutation.text_md: You are thinking that the $y$-intercept is where $y=0$, so you set $y=0$ to find it. Part of that is right: each intercept is found by setting one of the two letters to $0$. The slip is only in which letter.

The $y$-intercept is where the graph meets the $y$-axis, and every point on the $y$-axis has $x=0$. So to find the $y$-intercept you let $x=0$ and solve for $y$. That is exactly what the statement says, so the statement is true.

Try it on $y=x-1$. Let $x=0$: $y=(0)-1=-1$, so the $y$-intercept is $-1$, the point $(0, -1)$. Now let $y=0$: $0=x-1$, so $x=1$, the point $(1, 0)$, which is the $x$-intercept. Setting $y=0$ for the $y$-intercept would have given $1$, so your two answers would come out the wrong way round.

To keep them straight: for the $y$-intercept set $x=0$, and for the $x$-intercept set $y=0$. The letter you set to $0$ is always the other one. Then check the points: the $y$-intercept has $0$ as its first number, like $(0, -1)$, and the $x$-intercept has $0$ as its second, like $(1, 0)$.

entries.label: Matches the size of a but not its sign
entries.description: The student picks a parabola that opens the wrong way for the equation, letting the size of $a$ steer the choice while the sign of $a$ does not decide whether the curve goes up or down.
entries.signal: Chooses a curve that opens upward for an equation with a negative $a$, or downward for an equation with a positive $a$.

refutation.text_md: You were weighing up how wide or narrow each curve is, and the sign of $a$ (the plus or minus in front of $x^2$) did not get to decide which way the parabola goes. The size of $a$ is part of the job; the sign is the other part, and it tells you up or down.

Compare $y=2x^2$ with $y=-2x^2$. At $x=2$ the first gives $y=2\times 4=8$ and the second gives $y=-2\times 4=-8$. Same size, opposite sign, so every point of one is the mirror image of a point on the other: $y=-2x^2$ is the reflection of $y=2x^2$ in the $x$-axis.
When the equation is just $y=ax^2$, the turning point is at the origin. A positive $a$ keeps the whole curve above the $x$-axis, and a negative $a$ keeps it below.
So settle the direction first: read the sign of $a$ and cross out every curve that goes the other way. Then use the size of $a$ to choose between the curves that are left.

entries.label: Reverses which way the size of a changes the width
entries.description: The student thinks a larger number in front of $x^2$ makes the parabola wider and a smaller number makes it narrower, so they pick the curve at the opposite end of the width order from the right one.
entries.signal: Picks the flattest curve for the largest $a$, or the narrowest curve for the smallest $a$ (ignoring minus signs), among curves that open the right way.

refutation.text_md: You have the right idea that $a$ controls how wide the parabola is, but the effect has been turned the wrong way round. A bigger number in front of $x^2$ does not spread the curve out; it squeezes it in. It is an easy one to flip, because "bigger" sounds like "wider".

Test it with a point. Put $x=2$ into $y=0.5x^2$ and into $y=3x^2$: $0.5\times 4=2$ and $3\times 4=12$. At the same $x$, the larger $a$ gives a much higher $y$, so that curve climbs faster and is the narrower one.

It works the same below the $x$-axis if you ignore the minus sign. At $x=2$, $y=-2x^2$ gives $-8$ and $y=-0.75x^2$ gives $-3$. The curve with the bigger size of $a$ is further from the $x$-axis, so it is the narrower one.

So the larger the size of $a$, the narrower the parabola; the smaller, the wider and flatter. To choose, put an $x$-value you can read off the graph (such as 1 or 2) into the equation, work out $y$, and pick the curve that passes through that point.

entries.label: Shifts the parabola the wrong way for the sign of q
entries.description: The student reads a $+q$ as moving the parabola down and a $-q$ as moving it up, so they pick the curve shifted in the opposite direction.
entries.signal: Picks the curve whose turning point is below the origin for a positive $q$, or above the origin for a negative $q$.

refutation.text_md: You know the number at the end moves the whole parabola up or down; it is the direction that has been swapped, so a plus sent the curve down and a minus sent it up.

Find the turning point by putting $x=0$ into the equation. For $y=x^2+1$ you get $y=0+1=1$, so the turning point is $(0, 1)$, above the origin. For $y=x^2-3$ you get $y=0-3=-3$, so the turning point is $(0, -3)$, below it.

That number is $q$, and it is the $y$-intercept: the height where the curve crosses the $y$-axis. A positive $q$ is above the origin and a negative $q$ is below it, so $+q$ moves the parabola up and $-q$ moves it down, whatever $a$ is.
So read $q$ together with its sign, find $(0, q)$ on the $y$-axis, and pick the curve whose turning point sits there.

entries.label: Matches the x² part and ignores q
entries.description: The student picks the curve through the origin, matching only the $x^2$ part of the equation and treating the number added or subtracted at the end as if it did not move the graph.
entries.signal: Picks the curve whose turning point is at the origin for an equation that has a number added or subtracted at the end.

refutation.text_md: You matched the $x^2$ part, which gives the parabola its shape, and that part is right. The number at the end is $q$, and it moves the whole parabola up or down, so it cannot be skipped.
Put $x=0$ into $y=x^2+1$: $y=0+1=1$. The plain $y=x^2$ gives $y=0$ at $x=0$. The turning points are $(0, 1)$ and $(0, 0)$, so these are different curves.

When the curves have the same shape, as the ones in your question do, $q$ is the only thing that tells them apart. A turning point at the origin means $q=0$, and that is only true when nothing is added or subtracted at the end.
So find $q$ first: it is the height of the turning point on the $y$-axis. Pick the curve whose turning point is at $(0, q)$.

entries.label: Does not reverse the inequality when $a$ is negative
entries.description: When finding the range of $f(x)=ax^2+q$ with $a<0$, the student multiplies $x^2\geq0$ by $a$ but keeps the $\geq$ sign, so writes the range as $f(x)\geq q$ instead of $f(x)\leq q$.
entries.signal: For a parabola with $a<0$, the range is given as $f(x)\geq q$ (or $[q,\infty)$) instead of $f(x)\leq q$ (or $(-\infty,q]$).

refutation.text_md: You started in the right place: $x^2\geq0$, because a square is never negative. The slip comes next. You multiplied by $a$ and kept the $\geq$ sign. That is fine when $a$ is positive, but here $a<0$, and multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses its sign.
Test it with numbers. Take $a=-2$ and $x=3$. Then $x^2=9$ and $ax^2=-18$, which is below $0$, not above it. So $ax^2\geq0$ cannot be true. The correct statement is $ax^2\leq0$.
Adding $q$ to both sides does not change the direction, so $ax^2+q\leq q$. Every output $f(x)$ is at most $q$, so the range is $\left\{f(x):f(x)\leq q\right\}$, that is $(-\infty,q]$.
Next time, write the steps in order: $x^2\geq0$; multiply by $a$ and, if $a<0$, reverse the sign; then add $q$. The sign you end with is the direction of the range.

entries.label: Gives the range as all real numbers, like the domain
entries.description: The student sees that $x$ can be any real number and so writes the range as all real numbers too, instead of asking which outputs $f(x)$ the function can actually give.
entries.signal: For $y=ax^2+q$, the range is written as $(-\infty,\infty)$ or "all real numbers", the same as the domain.

refutation.text_md: You have the domain right: it is $\left\{x:x\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$, because there is no value of $x$ that makes the function undefined. But the domain is about the inputs, while the range is about the outputs $f(x)$ that actually come out. Outputs can be limited even when every input is allowed.
What limits the outputs here is the square. For every $x$ we have $x^2\geq0$. Then each step of the function acts on that inequality. Take $g(x)=x^2+2$: adding $2$ gives $x^2+2\geq2$, so $g(x)\geq2$.

So the outputs never go below $2$. An output of $1$, for example, would need $x^2=-1$, and no real number does that. The range is $\left\{g(x):g(x)\geq2\right\}$, not all real numbers, while the domain stays $\left\{x:x\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$.

Answer the two questions separately. Domain: which $x$ can go in? Range: start from $x^2\geq0$ and apply the function's steps to that inequality (multiply by $a$, reversing the sign if $a<0$, then add $q$) to see which outputs are possible.

entries.label: Thinking a continuous graph is one with breaks
entries.description: The student takes 'continuous' to describe a graph that has breaks, mixing it up with 'discontinuity', the word for the break in a hyperbola.

refutation.text_md: You have noticed something true: the graph of a hyperbola really does have a break in it. The slip is in which word goes with that break. It is easy to attach "continuous" to the breaks, because they are the part that stands out.
Look at $y=\frac{1}{x}$. It is drawn as two separate curves, with a gap at $x=0$ because $y$ is undefined there. The book calls that break a discontinuity at $x=0$.

So a graph with a break is the discontinuous one. A continuous graph is the opposite: a graph with no breaks in it. That makes the statement false, because a graph is continuous if there are no breaks in it.
Next time, check the graph for breaks first. No breaks means continuous. A break, like the gap at $x=0$ on a hyperbola, means a discontinuity.

entries.label: Thinking the graph meets its asymptote
entries.description: The student pictures an asymptote as a line the graph runs up to and touches or crosses, rather than a line it gets closer and closer to but never meets.

refutation.text_md: You are right that a curve gets very close to its asymptote, and on a sketch it can look as if the two meet. The mix-up is thinking the curve eventually reaches the line.

Take $y=\frac{1}{x}$, which we can also write as $x\times y=1$. Its asymptotes are $y=0$ and $x=0$. As $x$ gets larger, $y$ gets closer to $0$ but does not equal $0$. A point on the line $y=0$ would need $x\times 0=1$, which cannot happen.

The same goes for $x=0$. The function is undefined when $x=0$, so no point of the graph has $x=0$. The graph only gets closer and closer to the $y$-axis as $x$ gets closer to $0$. That is also why the graph is two separate curves.
So an asymptote is a straight line that a graph will never intersect, not one it intersects at least once, and the statement is false.
To test a line, ask whether any point of the graph can sit on it. For a hyperbola such as $y=\frac{1}{x}$, the lines $y=0$ and $x=0$ have no such point, and that is what marks them as asymptotes.

entries.label: Ignores the sign of a when choosing the curve
entries.description: The student chooses a curve in the wrong pair of quadrants for the sign of $a$, usually by matching on the number alone, so a negative $a$ gets a first-and-third-quadrant curve or a positive $a$ gets a second-and-fourth-quadrant one.
entries.signal: Picks or describes a graph in the second and fourth quadrants for a positive $a$, or in the first and third quadrants for a negative $a$.

refutation.text_md: It is easy to match on the number in the equation and let the sign slip past. The sign is worth checking first, because it decides which pair of quadrants the graph lies in, and that rules curves out straight away.

Test it the way the book fills in a table of values. For $y=\frac{2}{x}$: $x=1$ gives $y=2$ and $x=-1$ gives $y=-2$, so the points are $(1, 2)$ and $(-1, -2)$, top right and bottom left, which are the first and third quadrants. For $y=-\frac{2}{x}$: $x=1$ gives $y=-2$ and $x=-1$ gives $y=2$, so the points are $(1, -2)$ and $(-1, 2)$, bottom right and top left, which are the second and fourth quadrants.

The book states the rule the same way: when $a$ is positive the graph lies in the first and third quadrants, and when $a$ is negative it lies in the second and fourth. Changing only the sign of $a$ is a reflection on the $x$-axis, so $y=-\frac{2}{x}$ is the mirror image of $y=\frac{2}{x}$: the same size, in the other pair of quadrants. A curve in the wrong pair of quadrants cannot be right, however well its size seems to match.
Next time, look at the sign of $a$ first and rule out every curve in the wrong pair of quadrants. Only then use the size of $a$ to choose among the curves that are left.

entries.label: Right quadrants, wrong size of curve
entries.description: The student gets the pair of quadrants right from the sign of $a$ but picks a curve at the wrong distance from the axes, so the size of $a$ has not been matched to how far the graph sits from the axes.

refutation.text_md: Your quadrants are right, so the sign of $a$ is sorted. The curves left in those quadrants look alike and differ only in the size of $a$, which decides how far the graph sits from the axes. That is worth testing with a number rather than by eye.

A bigger $a$ pushes the graph farther from the axes, and a smaller $a$ brings it closer. Take $x=2$: $y=\frac{2}{x}$ gives $y=1$, but $y=\frac{8}{x}$ gives $y=4$. The point $(2, 4)$ is farther out, so it lies on the curve for $\frac{8}{x}$, not on the curve for $\frac{2}{x}$. Picking a curve of the wrong size means picking a point the equation never gives.
The book puts the same idea in words: $y=\frac{3}{x}$ is a magnification by $3$ of $y=\frac{1}{x}$, and $y=\frac{1}{2x}$ is a reduction by $2$ of it.
Next time, once the sign has told you the quadrants, put a convenient $x$ from the graph, such as $x=2$, into the equation. Work out $y$, mark that point, and choose the curve that passes through it.

entries.description: The student correctly leaves $x=0$ out of the domain, then gives the range as $g(x)\ne 0$ as well, treating the value the $y$-values must avoid as the same number as the value the $x$-values must avoid.
entries.signal: The range is written as $\left\{g(x):g(x)\in\mathbb{R},g(x)\ne0\right\}$ for a function like $g(x)=\frac{2}{x}+2$, or the domain and range are given as the same set.

refutation.text_md: You have the domain right: $x$ cannot be $0$, because $\frac{2}{x}$ is undefined there. The slip is carrying that same number across to the range. The two ask different things: the domain is about which $x$-values are allowed in, the range is about which $y$-values the graph actually reaches.

Look at $g(x)=\frac{2}{x}+2$. The fraction $\frac{2}{x}$ is never equal to $0$, whatever $x$ you choose. So $g(x)$, which is that fraction plus $2$, can never be exactly $2$. The $y$-value that is missing is $2$, the number added on at the end, not $0$.

You can also check that $0$ is not the missing $y$-value. For a graph like $y=\frac{3}{x}+2$, put $y=0$ and multiply both sides by $x$: $0=3+2x$, so $x=-\frac{3}{2}$. The graph meets the $x$-axis at $\left(-\frac{3}{2}, 0\right)$, so it does reach $y=0$. A value the graph reaches cannot be left out of the range.

Use two separate questions each time. Domain: which $x$ makes the denominator $0$? Here $x=0$, so $\left\{x:x\in\mathbb{R},x\ne0\right\}$. Range: which $y$-value can the graph never take? It is the number added at the end, here $2$, so $\left\{g(x):g(x)\in\mathbb{R},g(x)\ne2\right\}$.

refutation.text_md: You are remembering something true: the graph of $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}$ is the reflection of the graph of $y=2^{x}$. The slip is in which line plays which part. The line a graph is reflected about and the line a curve keeps getting closer to are two different jobs.

Find the line of reflection from the table of values. For $y=2^{x}$, the values at $x=-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$ are $\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{2}, 1, 2, 4$. For $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}$ they are $4, 2, 1, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}$, the same numbers in the opposite order. So each point $(x, y)$ on one graph has a partner $(-x, y)$ on the other, at the same height on the opposite side of the $y$-axis. The graphs are reflections of each other about the $y$-axis, which is why $y=2^{x}$ reflected about the $y$-axis gives $y=2^{-x}$, and both graphs pass through $(0, 1)$ on that axis.

The $x$-axis cannot be that line. Both graphs have $y>0$ at every point, so all of each graph sits above the $x$-axis and no point is below it. Reflecting about the $x$-axis would send points above it to points below it, and neither graph has any.

The $x$-axis does a different job. For $y=2^{x}$, moving left through $x=-2, -1, \dots$ the values get smaller and smaller, closer and closer to $0$, but you can never get $0$ by raising a non-zero number to a power, so the graph never touches the $x$-axis. The same happens to $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}$ as $x$ increases. A line that the curve approaches but never touches is an asymptote, and here its equation is $y=0$.

Next time, ask two questions. Does the curve keep getting closer to this line without ever touching it? Then it is an asymptote, and for these graphs that is the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Is one graph the reflection of the other about this line? For $y=b^{x}$ and $y=\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{x}$ that line is the $y$-axis.

entries.label: Starts the range at 0 whatever $q$ is
entries.description: The student remembers that $b^x$ is always positive and gives the range of $y=ab^x+q$ as $y>0$, forgetting that the $+q$ moves the line the range starts from to $y=q$.
entries.signal: A range of $y>0$ or $(0, \infty)$ given for a function with a positive $a$ and a nonzero $q$, such as $g(x)>0$ for $g(x)=5\cdot2^x+1$.

refutation.text_md: You have remembered that $2^x$ is always positive, so the values stay above 0 - that part is right. The slip is stopping there: the $+1$ in $5\cdot2^x+1$ changes every value, so it changes where the range starts.
Follow the book's chain of inequalities one line at a time. $2^x>0$. Multiplying by 5 keeps it positive: $5\times2^x>0$. Now add 1 to both sides: $5\times2^x+1>1$.
So $g(x)$ is always bigger than 1. A value such as $0.5$ is below 1, so it can never come out of $g$ - yet $y>0$ would allow it. That is where the two answers disagree.
The range is $\{g(x):g(x)>1\}$: it starts at the line $y=q$ (here $y=1$), not at 0.
Next time, start from $b^x>0$. When $a$ is positive, multiply by $a$, then add $q$ to both sides. The number you reach next to the $>$ sign is where the range starts.

entries.label: Puts the range above $y=q$ even when $a$ is negative
entries.description: The student reads the range as lying above the line $y=q$ whatever the sign of $a$, so for $y=-2^x$ they give $(0, \infty)$ instead of $(-\infty, 0)$.
entries.signal: The same range, $(0, \infty)$, given for both $y=2^x$ and $y=-2^x$.

refutation.text_md: You know that $2^x$ is always positive, and you have carried that straight over to $-2^x$ - a sensible starting point. What it misses is the minus sign in front: here $a=-1$, and the sign of $a$ decides whether the range lies above or below the line $y=q$.
Test one value. When $x=0$, $2^0=1$, so $y=-2^0=-1$. That is a negative number, and $(0, \infty)$ contains no negative numbers, so it cannot be the range of $y=-2^x$.

For every $x$, the value of $-2^x$ is the negative of the value of $2^x$. Since $2^x$ is always above 0, $-2^x$ is always below 0. So $y=2^x$ has range $(0, \infty)$ and $y=-2^x$ has range $(-\infty, 0)$ - different ranges, because the graphs are on opposite sides of the $x$-axis.
Before you write a range, look at the sign of $a$. A positive $a$ puts the range above $y=q$; a negative $a$ puts it below $y=q$. Then write the interval from there.

entries.label: Writes a square bracket or $\geq$ at the line $y=q$
entries.description: The student counts the line $y=q$ as part of the range of an exponential function, writing $[0, \infty)$ or $y\geq q$, as if the curve reached that line.
entries.signal: A range written with a square bracket or $\geq$ at the boundary, such as $[0, \infty)$ for $y=2^x$ or $g(x)\geq1$ for $g(x)=5\cdot2^x+1$.

refutation.text_md: You have the right starting value - 0 for $y=2^x$, 1 for $5\cdot2^x+1$ - and the right direction. The slip is the bracket: a square bracket or $\geq$ says the curve actually reaches that value.
Check whether it does. The book's first line is $2^x>0$ with a strict sign, because $2^x$ is never equal to 0. Carrying the strict sign through gives $5\times2^x+1>1$, so $g(x)$ is never equal to 1.

So there is no $x$ that gives the value at the boundary: 1 is not in the range of $g$, and 0 is not in the range of $y=2^x$. That is why the book writes $\{g(x):g(x)>1\}$ and $(0, \infty)$, with a round bracket.

For these exponential functions use a round bracket, or $>$ or $<$, at the line $y=q$: for example $(0, \infty)$ and $(-\infty, 0)$. Each time, ask: is there an $x$ that gives this value? If not, the bracket is round.

entries.label: Guesses the y-intercept instead of working it out
entries.description: The student takes the y-intercept straight from the numbers in the equation, either reading the number raised to the power $x$ as the height where the curve crosses the y-axis or assuming every such graph crosses at $(0, 1)$, instead of letting $x=0$.
entries.signal: Says the graph of $y=2^x$ crosses the y-axis at $(0, 2)$, or that the graph of $y=2\cdot2^x$ crosses it at $(0, 1)$.

refutation.text_md: You have worked out where the curve crosses the y-axis by looking at the numbers in the equation, rather than by calculating it. The y-intercept does depend on those numbers, but it is not the number being raised to the power $x$, and it is not always $1$ either.
The book finds the y-intercept by letting $x=0$ and working out $y$. Any number raised to the power $0$ is $1$, so the power part of the equation becomes $1$ at $x=0$.
Take $y=2^x$. At $x=0$, $y=2^0=1$. The curve crosses the y-axis at $(0, 1)$, not at $(0, 2)$.

Now put a multiplier in front, $y=2\cdot2^x$. At $x=0$, $y=2\cdot2^0=2\cdot1=2$, so this curve crosses at $(0, 2)$. The multiplier $a$ is what moves the intercept, so the curve through $(0, 1)$ belongs to the equation without it.
A minus sign follows the same rule. $y=-2^x$ gives $y=-2^0=-1$, so it crosses at $(0, -1)$, not at $(0, -2)$.

Next time, replace $x$ with $0$ in the whole equation, remember that the power becomes $1$, work out $y$ (adding $q$ if the equation has one), and choose the curve that crosses the y-axis at exactly that point.

entries.label: Swaps the rising and falling curves
entries.description: The student picks a curve that falls as $x$ increases for an equation whose number raised to the power $x$ is bigger than $1$ (like $2^x$), or one that rises for a number between $0$ and $1$ (like $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$), mixing up which numbers give which direction.
entries.signal: Picks a curve that falls for $y=2^x$ or $y=2\cdot2^x$, or one that rises for $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$.

refutation.text_md: You have picked a curve that heads the opposite way to the one this equation gives. Checking which way the curve goes is the right idea; it is just easy to mix up which numbers make a curve rise and which make it fall.
Test it with two values of $x$, as you would when plotting points. For $y=2^x$: $x=0$ gives $y=1$ and $x=1$ gives $y=2$. The $y$-value goes up, so the curve rises as $x$ increases.

For $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$: $x=0$ gives $y=1$ and $x=1$ gives $y=\frac{1}{2}$. The $y$-value goes down, so the curve falls as $x$ increases, getting closer and closer to its horizontal asymptote, the x-axis.

Both curves pass through $(0, 1)$, which is why they are easy to swap; only the direction tells them apart. With a positive multiplier in front, a number bigger than $1$ raised to the power $x$ gives a rising curve, and a number between $0$ and $1$ gives a falling one.
Before you choose, put $x=0$ and $x=1$ into the equation, see whether $y$ goes up or down, and pick the curve that does the same.

entries.label: Overlooks the minus sign in front of the power
entries.description: The student picks a curve above the x-axis for an equation with a minus sign in front of the power (such as $y=-2^x$ or $y=-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$), treating it as if the minus sign were not there or belonged to the exponent.
entries.signal: Picks a curve that lies above the x-axis for an equation that starts with a minus sign.

refutation.text_md: You have treated the equation as if the minus sign were not there, or as if it belonged up in the exponent. That is easy to do, because $2^x$ is the part that catches the eye. But the minus sign sits in front of the whole power, so it makes the multiplier $a$ negative.
When $a$ is negative, the graph lies below its horizontal asymptote. These equations have no $+q$, so the asymptote is the x-axis, $y=0$, and every point on the curve has a negative $y$-value.

Check with numbers. For $y=-2^x$: at $x=0$, $y=-2^0=-1$. For $y=-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$: at $x=0$, $y=-2\cdot1=-2$. Both cross the y-axis below the x-axis, so a curve that sits above the x-axis and crosses at a positive value cannot be right.
Before you choose, look at the sign of $a$. If it is negative, rule out every curve above the horizontal asymptote (here the x-axis), then use $x=0$ to choose between the curves that are left.

entries.label: Looks for an axis of symmetry on an exponential graph
entries.description: The student asks where the axis of symmetry of an exponential graph is, or tries to use one to place points when sketching, expecting a mirror line as on other graphs.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to look for an axis of symmetry, because some graphs you have met are mirror-shaped about a vertical line. The book states that exponential functions have no axis of symmetry, so there is no such line to find.

Take $y=3\times2^x+2$. On the left, the curve flattens out towards its horizontal asymptote, the line $y=2$. On the right, it climbs higher and higher. A mirror line would make the two sides match, and these two sides look nothing like each other.

A graph with a mirror line has pairs of points at the same height, one on each side. This curve never does: every height above $y=2$ occurs at only one $x$-value. For example, $y=5$ happens only at the y-intercept $(0, 5)$.

So do not look for a mirror line when you sketch. Use the book's steps instead: use the sign of $a$ and the value of $q$ to see which way the graph goes and where it sits, find the intercepts, draw the horizontal asymptote $y=q$, then plot the points and join them up.

entries.label: Amplitude given the sign of a
entries.description: When $a$ is negative, the student gives the amplitude as a negative number, reading it straight off $a$ (for example, saying the amplitude of $y=-2\sin\theta+1$ is $-2$).
entries.signal: An amplitude written as a negative number, such as $-2$.

refutation.text_md: You have read the amplitude straight off $a$. That works when $a$ is positive: for $y=2\sin\theta$ the amplitude is $2$. The slip is carrying the minus sign across when $a$ is negative.
The book's rule is that amplitude is always positive. It says how much the graph is stretched, and an amount of stretch is a size, not a direction, so it cannot be negative.

The minus sign in $a$ already has a job of its own: it reflects the graph in the $x$-axis. Take $y=-2\sin\theta+1$. Because $a=-2$, the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis, and the $2$ is the size of the stretch. Both facts are kept, in two different places.

Read $a$ in two parts. The sign tells you whether the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis. The size, with the minus sign dropped, is the amplitude. For $y=-2\sin\theta+1$ that gives: reflected, and amplitude $2$.

entries.label: Picks the basic sine graph and never applies a
entries.description: The student matches an equation such as $y=3\sin\theta$ or $y=\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta$ to the curve for plain $y=\sin\theta$, because every one of these graphs has the same sine shape, and so never applies the number in front of $\sin\theta$.
entries.signal: Chooses the curve whose maximum is $1$ (and minimum $-1$) for an equation whose $a$ is not $1$.

refutation.text_md: You started from the basic sine graph, and that is the right place to start: $\sin\theta$ is $0, 1, 0, -1, 0$ at $0^{\circ}, 90^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}, 270^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}$. But that is only the first step. The number in front of $\sin\theta$ still has to be applied to it.

When $q=0$, the graphs of $a\sin\theta$ all have the same shape and cross the $x$-axis at the same places, so the shape alone cannot tell them apart. What $a$ changes is the height: it multiplies every height of the basic graph.

Test it on $y=3\sin\theta$. At $90^{\circ}$ the basic graph is at $\sin 90^{\circ}=1$, so $3\sin\theta$ is at $3\times 1=3$. The graph is stretched, with a maximum of $3$ and a minimum of $-3$. The curve that peaks at $1$ belongs to $y=\sin\theta$ only, where $a=1$.

The move that works: find $a$ first, then apply it to the basic graph. With $q=0$ the maximum is $a$ and the minimum is $-a$. Choose the curve that has those values. If the number in front of $\sin\theta$ is not $1$, the curve that peaks at $1$ cannot be the match.

entries.label: Stretch and contraction the wrong way round
entries.description: The student takes a number greater than $1$ to squash the graph and a fraction between $0$ and $1$ to stretch it, so chooses a curve on the wrong side of the basic sine graph: a flatter curve for $y=2\sin\theta$ or $y=3\sin\theta$, a taller one for $y=\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta$.
entries.signal: For $a>1$, chooses a curve whose maximum is below $1$. For $0<a<1$, chooses a curve whose maximum is above $1$.

refutation.text_md: You know that $a$ changes the height of the basic sine graph, and that part is right. The slip is the direction: treating a number bigger than $1$ as squashing the graph and a fraction as stretching it.

Check it with heights. At $90^{\circ}$ the basic graph is at $\sin 90^{\circ}=1$, and $a\sin\theta$ is at $a\times 1$. For $y=2\sin\theta$ that is $2\times 1=2$, which is higher than $1$. So $a>1$ stretches the graph: the maximum is $2$ and the minimum is $-2$.

For $y=\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta$ the height at $90^{\circ}$ is $\frac{1}{2}\times 1=\frac{1}{2}$, which is lower than $1$. So a fraction between $0$ and $1$ contracts the graph: the maximum is $\frac{1}{2}$ and the minimum is $-\frac{1}{2}$. A curve that peaks at $2$ belongs to $y=2\sin\theta$, because multiplying by $\frac{1}{2}$ halves the heights and multiplying by $2$ doubles them.

The move that works: compare $a$ with $1$ first. If $a>1$ the graph is stretched and peaks above $1$. If $0<a<1$ it is contracted and peaks below $1$. Then confirm it by working out $a\times 1$. With $q=0$ that is the maximum, and you choose the curve with that peak.

entries.description: The student reads a off the equation and reports it, sign included, as the amplitude, so y = -4 cos θ is said to have amplitude -4 and the minus sign is treated as part of the size of the stretch.

refutation.text_md: You spotted that $a=-4$ in $y=-4\cos\theta$, which is the right first move. The slip is calling the amplitude $-4$, as if the amplitude and $a$ were the same thing.

The amplitude is a size, so it is always positive. Here $q=0$, so the graph is not shifted up or down. It reaches 4 units above the $x$-axis and 4 units below it: the maximum is $4$ and the minimum is $-4$. The amplitude is $4$.

The minus sign has not disappeared. It tells you the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis. Instead of starting at its highest point when $\theta=0^\circ$, this graph starts at its lowest: the $y$-intercept is $(0^\circ, -4)$, and the $x$-intercepts are $(90^\circ, 0)$ and $(270^\circ, 0)$. So $y=-4\cos\theta$ is stretched by 4 and reflected in the $x$-axis.

Next time, split $a$ into two jobs. The size of $a$ gives the amplitude, here $4$. The sign of $a$ tells you whether the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis, and a minus sign means it is. Then add $q$ to move the graph up or down. For $y=-2\cos\theta+1$ that gives amplitude $2$, reflected, and shifted up 1, so the maximum is $3$ and the minimum is $-1$.

entries.label: Takes the whole top-to-bottom distance as a
entries.description: The student subtracts the bottom y-value from the top y-value and gives that distance as a, without dividing by 2.
entries.signal: a comes out as the full height of the graph from bottom to top, which is double the amplitude.

refutation.text_md: You measured from the top of the graph to the bottom, and that is a good first move. The slip is stopping there: that distance is the whole height of the wave, and the whole height is not the amplitude.

The amplitude is the distance from the middle of the graph up to the top, or from the middle down to the bottom. The top-to-bottom distance covers both of those stretches, so it is twice the amplitude.

Take a graph whose top is at $y=-0.5$ and whose bottom is at $y=-1.5$. The distance from top to bottom is $-0.5-(-1.5)=1$. If $a=1$, the wave would reach 1 above its middle and 1 below it, so its top and bottom would be 2 apart, but this graph's top and bottom are only 1 apart. Halving gives $a=\frac{1}{2}$.
The move that works: when you are given the top and the bottom of the graph, work out $\frac{\text{top}-\text{bottom}}{2}$ to get $a$.

entries.label: Reads q as the height where the graph meets the y-axis
entries.description: The student takes the y-value at $0^\circ$ (the y-intercept) as q, forgetting that this value is $a+q$.
entries.signal: q equals the y-value of the point at $0^\circ$, so it is off by exactly a.

refutation.text_md: You read q from where the graph meets the y-axis, at $0^\circ$. That is a sensible place to look, and q does move the graph up or down. The catch is that this starting height is not q on its own.

An unshifted cosine graph $y=a\cos\theta$ starts at height $a$ when $\theta=0^\circ$, not at 0. So the y-intercept is $(0^\circ, a+q)$: the amplitude plus the shift. Reading it as q forgets that $a$ is already in that height.

Take a graph with $a=\frac{1}{2}$ that passes through $(0^\circ, -0.5)$. Trying $q=-0.5$ gives $y=\frac{1}{2}\cos\theta-0.5$, which at $0^\circ$ equals $0.5-0.5=0$, not $-0.5$. The graph would miss the point.

The move that works: compare with the unshifted graph $\frac{1}{2}\cos\theta$, which starts at $(0^\circ, 0.5)$. This graph starts at $-0.5$, which is 1 unit lower, so $q=-1$. In short, $q=(\text{y-value at }0^\circ)-a$, and here $-0.5-0.5=-1$.

entries.label: Gives q as the size of the shift and forgets its direction

entries.signal: q has the right size but the wrong sign: positive when the graph sits lower than the unshifted graph.

refutation.text_md: You compared the graph with the unshifted cosine graph and measured the shift correctly. What is missing is the direction: q is not just the distance moved.
In $y=a\cos\theta+q$, a positive q shifts the graph up and a negative q shifts it down. A graph that has moved down has a negative q.

Take a graph with $a=\frac{1}{2}$ that passes through $(0^\circ, -0.5)$. The unshifted graph $\frac{1}{2}\cos\theta$ starts at $(0^\circ, 0.5)$, so this graph is 1 unit lower. Test $q=1$: $\frac{1}{2}\cos 0^\circ+1=1.5$, which is above the point, not at $-0.5$. Test $q=-1$: $0.5-1=-0.5$, which matches the point.
The move that works: once you have the size of the shift, say whether it is up or down, and write q positive for up and negative for down. Then put the given point into $y=a\cos\theta+q$ to check.

entries.label: Gives the whole interval as the domain and forgets the asymptote angles
entries.description: The student writes the domain of a tangent graph as the full interval it is drawn over, such as $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$, without excluding the angles where the dashed vertical asymptotes sit.
entries.signal: A domain with no $\theta\ne$ condition, such as $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$, for a tangent graph drawn over that interval.

refutation.text_md: You have the right start: the graph is drawn from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$, so that interval is the first part of the domain. What is missing is the angles inside it where the graph has no points.

A tangent graph has dashed vertical lines, called asymptotes. The curve gets closer and closer to each one but never touches it, and it breaks there: one branch stops on one side and a new branch starts on the other. On a graph drawn from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$, such as $y=-\tan\theta$, the asymptotes are at $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and $\theta=270^{\circ}$.

The domain is the set of $\theta$-values the graph actually has points for. At $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and $\theta=270^{\circ}$ there is no point on the curve, so those two angles are not in the domain, even though they sit inside the interval. Your answer $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$ would wrongly include them.

The book's answer for $y=-\tan\theta$ keeps the interval and then removes the two asymptote angles: $\{\theta:0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ},\ \theta\ne90^{\circ},270^{\circ}\}$. The graphs of $y=\tan\theta+1$ and $y=\tan\theta-1$ over the same interval get the same two exclusions.
Next time: write the interval first, then look along the dashed lines inside it and add a $\theta\ne$ for each one.

Follow a branch towards a dashed vertical line (an asymptote). The closer it gets, the more steeply it climbs, or falls, past any height you name. It is only cut off at the edge of the picture. So no $y$-value is a top or a bottom of the graph.

Take the branch of $y=\tan\theta+1$ between the dashed lines at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$. On the left it heads down past the bottom of the picture, it passes through $E(180^{\circ},1)$, and on the right it heads up past the top. A range of $-8\le y\le8$ would leave out heights the curve really reaches.
The book gives the range of both $y=\tan\theta+1$ and $y=\tan\theta-1$ as $y\in\mathbb{R}$. The $+1$ or $-1$ slides the whole graph up or down, but it does not put a top or a bottom on it.
Next time: do not take the range from the edges of the drawing. If the branches keep running up or down beside the asymptotes, write $y\in\mathbb{R}$.
